title: Artificial Selection and Genetic Engineering
seo_title: Grade 8 Artificial Selection and Genetic Engineering Worksheets: Breeding and Genes
standard_text: Gather and synthesize information about the technologies that have changed the way humans influence the inheritance of desired traits in organisms.
meta_desc: Free middle school science worksheets on artificial selection and genetic engineering (NGSS MS-LS4-5): selective breeding, breeding data over generations, genetic engineering and gene therapy, and their benefits and risks. 100 practice questions with answers.
key_big: People can choose which traits are passed on.
key_sub: Selective breeding chooses parents over many generations. Genetic engineering changes genes directly. Both have benefits and risks.
body_html:
How to think about it

People influence which traits are inherited in two main ways:

  • Artificial selection (selective breeding): people choose parents with desired traits, generation after generation. Dogs from wolves, corn from teosinte and broccoli from wild mustard were made this way.
  • Genetic engineering: scientists change genes directly, often by adding a gene from another species (insulin-making bacteria, Bt corn, golden rice) or editing a gene (CRISPR). Gene therapy uses this to treat diseases.

These technologies have benefits (more food, medicine) and risks (low variation, resistance, health problems in some breeds).

Example

Breeders mate the fastest horses. Process?

People choose parents.

Answer: artificial selection

Example

A gene for insulin is added to bacteria. Process?

Genes changed directly.

Answer: genetic engineering

Common mistakes

  • Thinking selective breeding creates brand-new genes on purpose.
  • Thinking genetic engineering and natural selection are the same.
  • Thinking artificial selection works in one generation.

faq.q: What is the difference between artificial selection and genetic engineering?
faq.a: In artificial selection, people choose which organisms reproduce over many generations. In genetic engineering, scientists change an organism's genes directly.

faq.q: What are examples of artificial selection?
faq.a: Dog breeds from wolves, modern corn from teosinte, and broccoli, cabbage and kale from wild mustard.

faq.q: What are some risks of these technologies?
faq.a: Low genetic variation can make crops vulnerable to disease, pests can evolve resistance, and some breeds have health problems.

items.q: What is genetic engineering?
c: directly changing an organism's genes, often by adding a gene from another organism

items.q: Can artificial selection create a trait that has no genetic variation at all?
c: No. It can only select from traits that already vary.

items.q: Sofia reads: “A jellyfish gene for glowing protein is added to fish to make them glow.” Which process is this?
items.e: Scientists change or move genes directly.

items.q: Luis reads: “Farmers breed only the cows that give the most milk.” Which process is this?
Emma reads: “Moths with dark wings survive better on sooty trees with no human choosing.” Which process is this?
items.e: The environment, not people, decides which individuals survive.

items.q: What is gene therapy?
c: a type of surgery on bones
treating a disease by changing or replacing a faulty gene in a person's cells

items.q: Kai reads: “Scientists add genes to rice so it makes vitamin A (golden rice).” Which process is this?
items.e: Scientists change or move genes directly.

items.q: Ethan reads: “On an island, birds with stronger beaks survive a drought and reproduce.” Which process is this?
items.e: The environment, not people, decides which individuals survive.

items.q: Ben reads: “Gardeners save seeds from the sweetest tomatoes each year.” Which process is this?
What is artificial selection?
c: humans choosing which organisms reproduce to increase desired traits

items.q: Sam reads: “Breeders choose the chickens that lay the most eggs.” Which process is this?
Noah reads: “A gene from a soil bacterium is added to corn so it makes its own insect poison (Bt corn).” Which process is this?
items.e: Scientists change or move genes directly.

items.q: Lily reads: “Over thousands of years, people planted seeds from the biggest teosinte plants, producing modern corn.” Which process is this?
How is artificial selection different from natural selection?
c: People, not the environment, choose which traits are passed on.

items.q: Grace reads: “Bacteria become resistant to an antibiotic in a hospital.” Which process is this?
items.e: The environment, not people, decides which individuals survive.

items.q: Why might farmers want crops with less genetic variation?
c: The crops are uniform in size, taste and harvest time.

items.q: Ruby reads: “Scientists use CRISPR to edit a gene in a crop so it resists a disease.” Which process is this?
items.e: Scientists change or move genes directly.

items.q: Maya reads: “Horse breeders mate the fastest horses to produce racehorses.” Which process is this?
Why does selective breeding take many generations?
c: It always works in one generation.
Desired traits become more common a little at a time with each generation.
Genes are added slowly by hand.

items.q: What is one advantage of genetic engineering over selective breeding?
c: A specific gene can be added in one generation, even from another species.

items.q: Noah learns that dog breeds like poodles, beagles and huskies came from gray wolves. How did people get this result?
c: by natural selection with no human help
by genetic engineering in a single year
by artificial selection: breeding the individuals with desired traits for many generations
by mixing chemicals into the soil
